progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c04a and c04b (addition and its conditions; two products from an unsymmetrical alkene; UV substitution gives a mixture); chem-m7-c06 (hydration conditions; haloalkane plus aqueous NaOH under reflux; same carbon); chem-m7-c08a and c08b (dehydration, HX substitution, oxidation and the class rule; distil against reflux; aldehyde and ketone names); chem-m7-c09 (carboxylic acid names); chem-m7-c10 (esterification, conditions, equilibrium arrow, ester names, cutting an ester, the two-step flow chart, the main road); chem-m7-c11 (amide formation); chem-m7-c12 (saponification, map arrow only); chem-m7-c01 (naming and locants). Not assumed: reaction map, intermediate, dead end, working backwards, overall yield.
progression.startsWith: Choose a target functional group and starting material. The video opens: Propyl ethanoate is an ester that smells a lot like pears. Suppose the only carbon compounds you're allowed to start from are ethene, a gas, and 1-bromopropane, a haloalkane. Neither one looks anything like the ester.
progression.stopsAfter: building a reaction map; counting carbons; working backwards from a target; choosing a route by position and by conditions; drawing a multi-step flow chart (including two arms that join) with reagents, conditions and named intermediates; spotting arrows that don't exist. No mechanisms, no reductions, no yield calculations.

teaching.task: You want a pear-scented ester, but all you have is a gas and a haloalkane. How do you plan a route from the compounds you have to the one you want, and show it as a flow chart?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the target and the starting materials look nothing alike, so the route needs planning (1); (2) every reaction met so far sits on one map; the alcohol is the hub (2); (3) the reactions change groups and keep chains, so count carbons first; only ester and amide formation join chains (3); (4) work backwards: ask which reaction makes the target's group, then repeat (4); (5) choose: a haloalkane that already has its halogen on the right carbon fixes the position of the OH, because hydroxide takes the halogen's place on the same carbon, while water or HBr on propene goes mainly to the middle carbon (5); (6) write forwards, in the order you'd carry it out, with every reagent and condition; reflux with excess oxidant reaches the acid because the aldehyde can't escape (c08a recall); hydration and esterification are equilibria (6); (7) check: no direct alkane to alcohol arrow; a ketone has no H on its carbonyl carbon, so no further oxidation, and the acid needs the primary alcohol; each step loses product, so shorter routes usually yield more (7); memory aid (8); two attempts and brief feedback (9 to 12); handoff (13); key notes (14).
teaching.conversationalApproach: a pear-scented ester, propyl ethanoate, has to be made when the only carbon compounds allowed are ethene, a gas, and 1-bromopropane, so the video asks how to plan a route from the compounds you have to the one you want and show it as a flow chart. Every reaction met so far sits on one reaction map of nine families, with the alcohol as the hub. Move one names the functional group in the target and in each starting material and counts carbons, because the reactions change groups and keep chains, and only ester or amide formation joins two chains. Move two works backwards from the target: an ester comes from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, so the ester is cut into propan-1-ol and ethanoic acid. Move three chooses the route where position matters: hydroxide puts the OH where the bromine was in 1-bromopropane, while hydrating propene would put it on the wrong carbon. Move four writes the route forwards with reagents and conditions on every arrow (ethene and steam with a phosphoric acid catalyst, ethanol oxidised to ethanoic acid, the esterification), and every arrow is checked, because one wrong arrow breaks the route, shown with a plan for propanoic acid that fails twice. The memory aid is work backwards to plan, write forwards to answer. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Propyl ethanoate is an ester that smells a lot like pears. Suppose the only carbon compounds you're allowed to start from are ethene, a gas, and 1-bromopropane, a haloalkane. Neither one looks anything like the ester. Making a target compound from simpler ones is called a synthesis. So how do you plan a route from what you have to what you want, and show it as a flow chart?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A chemist wants to make pentanoic acid, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂COOH. The only available starting materials are pent-1-ene and 1-chloropentane. Construct a flow chart for a two-step synthesis from the better starting material. Include the reagents and conditions for each step, name the intermediate, and justify your choice of starting material." New compounds (no pent-1-ene against 1-chloropentane task on site L19 or L20, checked by phrase 27 Oct); a planning task that practises move 3 (choose by position), c06's same carbon, the class rule (primary to acid) and reflux with excess oxidant (learning L5). Crossed mistake: "pent-1-ene → (steam) → pentan-2-ol → pentanoic acid" (a secondary alcohol gives a ketone). (A2) "A chemist has only ethene and butan-1-ol as carbon-containing starting materials. Draw a flow chart to make ethyl butanoate, CH₃CH₂CH₂COOCH₂CH₃. Show the reagents and conditions on every arrow." New target and start pair (Revision 1's ethyl propanoate from ethene and propan-1-ol matched the site's L19 MC Q1 option C; site L19 and L20 have no ethyl butanoate synthesis, checked by phrase 27 Oct); tests the ester cut and naming order (c10), which starting material is oxidised, reflux with excess oxidant, and equilibrium arrows. Crossed mistake: oxidising the ethanol and esterifying with butan-1-ol, which makes butyl ethanoate, an isomer with the same formula C₆H₁₂O₂.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "draft and construct flow charts to show reaction pathways for chemical synthesis, including those that involve more than one step" This video covers planning a multi-step synthesis from a target and its allowed starting materials, and drawing it as a flow chart with every reagent and condition. Chem-m7-c10 introduced the flow chart with one two-step route; chem-m7-g03 practises harder targets. this video starts by choosing a target functional group and the starting materials, and stops at a justified multi-step pathway with conditions. It teaches: the reactions from c04a to c12 sit on one reaction map, each box a functional group family and each arrow a known reaction with its own reagents and conditions; the alcohol is the hub, so many routes pass through it; a four-move method: (1) name the functional groups in the target and the starting materials and count carbons (these reactions change functional groups and keep the chain length; only ester and amide formation join two molecules, so their carbons add); (2) work backwards from the target, asking which reaction makes its group (an ester comes from an acid and an alcohol, cut at the single-bonded oxygen; an acid from a primary alcohol by oxidation; an alcohol from an alkene and steam, or from a haloalkane), until you reach a starting material; (3) choose between possible routes: when the position of a group matters, start from a haloalkane that already has its halogen on the right carbon, because hydroxide takes the halogen's place on the same carbon, while water or HBr on propene can go on either carbon and goes mainly to the middle one, so it gives mainly the wrong product (Revision 2); (4) write the route forwards as a flow chart, in the order you'd carry it out, a compound in each box with its name, reagents and conditions on each arrow, distillation for an aldehyde and reflux with excess oxidant for an acid, an equilibrium arrow for hydration and esterification; then check every arrow: no single step turns an alkane into an alcohol (halogen and UV light first, giving a mixture); a ketone has no hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon, so acidified dichromate doesn't oxidise it further (a dead end), and a tertiary alcohol doesn't oxidise at all; each step loses some product, so a shorter route usually gives a higher overall yield; worked example: propyl ethanoate from ethene and 1-bromopropane, two arms (ethene → ethanol → ethanoic acid; 1-bromopropane → propan-1-ol) joining at esterification. Not here: reaction mechanisms and the words nucleophile and elimination as mechanisms (author note b); alcoholic NaOH elimination (not shown in this video from Revision 2; author note b); Markovnikov's rule by name (c04a author note b; author note c; the narration says only that propene's product is mainly the middle-carbon one); reduction reactions and reagents such as LiAlH₄ (not Module 7; author note d); the five-component "top-band" answer template and conditions-table timing drills (site L20; author note e); isolation and purification after each step (c10 and p05; one grey chip only); yield calculations (author note f); industrial synthesis such as aspirin (site hook; site correction 2); the practice set (chem-m7-g03).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c08a and c10: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; oxygen brick red, the OH ringed red; the C=C teal; bromine deep orange-brown; the carbonyl C=O with its second bond line red; condition chips navy on and under each arrow; the equilibrium arrow navy with two half heads; source-video chips grey; the chosen path amber; a crossed arrow dashed grey with a red cross. Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Target", "Map", "1 Count", "2 Backwards", "3 Choose", "4 Forwards", "Check"); centre the structure or flow chart board, one model at a time; the reaction map small at the right as a grey card once built; plates small at the left or right only in scenes 1, 12 and 13 (Revision 2). Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once (the map counts as one dimmed reference diagram, with only the current path bright); every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous model leaves before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 27 Oct): `m7-ester-fruit-v1.png` (a banana, a pineapple and a pear in watercolour and ink; scenes 1, 12 and 13, small; a coded ring marks the pear in scenes 1 and 13 and the pineapple in scene 12). Scaled uniformly only, never stretched. Not used from Revision 2: `m7-reflux-apparatus-v1.png` and `m7-school-distillation-setup-v1.png` (inspected 27 Oct; learning L3). No human figures.
design.transitionPlan: The ester fruit plate opens the hook with the target ester and the two starting materials as boxes and a gap between them; the board clears as the reaction map places its nine family boxes one at a time, then draws its arrows with the alcohol hub ringed; the target and starting boxes return with their groups ringed and carbon counters ticking; working backwards, the ester splits at its single-bonded oxygen into an acid box and an alcohol box with arrows drawn right to left; 1-bromopropane's bromine lifts off and an OH docks on the same carbon, then propene's two-way docker ghosts the OH on carbon one and bolds it on the middle carbon; the flow chart builder runs left to right with condition chips on each arrow and a name in each box; a failing flow chart for propanoic acid draws and its two wrong arrows are ringed and crossed; the memory lines write; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the card as the flow chart builds box by box and a crossed chip lands; the memory lines and the full reaction map card return with the next chip; scene crossfade with settle.
